subject: system-design
title: Fault Tolerance
summary: Faults are inevitable; the goal is to keep the system working correctly anyway, so a fault never becomes a failure the user sees.

blocks.text: In a large system, something is always broken: a disk dies, a process hangs, a network link drops. Fault tolerance is the design discipline of continuing to operate correctly despite these faults, rather than assuming they won't happen.

A fault is one component deviating from spec; a failure is the system as a whole stopping its service to the user. The point of fault tolerance is to break the chain between them. A fault should be absorbed quietly, never escalating into a failure the user notices.
You tolerate a component dying by having another ready to take its place. Redundancy comes in two flavors that trade cost against recovery time.

items: In active-active, all replicas serve traffic; losing one just sheds a fraction of capacity.
In active-passive (failover), a standby waits idle and is promoted when the primary fails.
Active-active hides faults seamlessly but costs more; failover is cheaper but adds a detect-and-promote gap.

blocks.title: No single point of failure
blocks.text: Trace every request path and ask: what one component, if it died, takes the whole system down? Each such single point of failure must be made redundant or it defines your ceiling on reliability.

A backup is only useful if it has the data. Replication keeps copies in sync so a standby can take over without losing state, and checkpointing periodically saves progress so a recovered component can resume rather than restart from scratch.

When you can't fully tolerate a fault, degrade instead of collapsing. Shed the non-essential so the core service survives: serve stale cache data, disable a recommendation panel, queue writes for later. A reduced experience beats an error page.

Put together, fault tolerance is layered: eliminate single points of failure, replicate state, fail over fast, and degrade gracefully when all else strains. The user should never learn which part broke.
